utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. I'm sorry there was a little delay with the recording equipment becoming ready. May I remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Polovina, good morning. I would like to introduce myself. I am attorney Bulatovic and I am one of the Defence attorneys for Mr. Sljivancanin. All of the warnings or cautions given to you by my colleagues during the questioning regarding the interpretation are valid so that we can do a good job and that it also gets recorded in the transcript. So please pay attention to that. Yesterday you talked about your stay in Vukovar and about your work at Radio Vukovar. Could you please clarify, because I see in the statement that you gave to the representatives of the OTP, that there is a kind of break or interruption in your work. And yesterday you said that you were not permanently employed. So I'm interested, when did you work, if you can tell us the time permanent, and when was it that you were permanently employed?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I came to the radio was on the 11th of July, 1997 [as interpreted]. I don't know how long this period lasted. I was substituting for a colleague, Mirjana Hrpka, who was an anchor there for many years. She had to go on sick leave, so it was necessary to replace her, and I was called by Radio Vukovar and offered this job. I think that this lasted until 1990. After that, my colleague came back from her sick leave and I stopped working at this part-time job. After the auditions were held in June 1991 I returned to work at the radio again. It was not a permanent job but a temporary job. I was offered a permanent position on the 1st of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This period, from the end of 1990 until 1991, did you do any work? And if you were employed, what were you doing and where?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I wasn't working other than perhaps giving maths lessons, but I it wasn't actually employed anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Just one intervention on the transcript. Page 2, line 4, it says "July 1997," but I think it should state July 1990, if I'm not mistaken. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I say "1997" or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, you said it correctly, but this is in the transcript. Well, it's all fine now. This period that I'm asking you about when you were not working, at that time did you go and visit people who were working at Radio Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion or those occasions, did you have any kind of active role in the Radio Vukovar programme in terms of advice or perhaps doing some project or providing suggestions or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I helped by -- actually, we're talking about music shows or music programmes. When Sinisa Glavasevic and Branimir Polovina were working, then the listeners would call in. These were music programmes and listeners were able to call in and make requests. And these requests would be granted. The songs would be played. So it was possible to grant listeners' requests because I knew practically where every record or every song was. I know -- I knew the number of each song. There are about 16.000 songs. Sinisa would talk with the listener. I would go to the record that the listener had requested. I would take it. Branko would put it on the record-player, and then it would be employed. That was the extent of my help.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You've explained that. But now I'm interested in knowing at the time, after having only worked for six months, how could you know where all of these 16.000 records were? How was it possible for you to achieve this? How did you manage to do that? It's a large number of songs.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a large number of songs but since I was an amateur singer, I was very interested in that topic and I simply remembered -- managed to memorise all the songs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Out of 16.000 records you knew exactly which one was where?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you said that that was what you were doing when Sinisa Glavasevic and Branko Polovina were doing their shift?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us what Sinisa Glavasevic was doing and what Branko Polovina were doing?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sinisa Glavasevic and Branislav Polovina -- actually, Sinisa Glavasevic was an anchor at Radio Vukovar, so he anchored the programmes. Branko or Branimir Polovina was a technician. So they worked together as a team.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Sinisa Glavasevic, you said that he was an anchor at Radio Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All the time until November 11th, 1991, did he work as an anchor? Did he continue to work as an anchor throughout that period in conditions that permitted such work?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was also a journalist. He was employed as an anchor, but in due time he also became a journalist and then later he became an editor at the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You already talked about this, but in order to be more specific do you know the date when he was appointed editor?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was probably the -- July or August of 1991. In any case, it was in the second half of the year after the war had already started.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: After being appointed to this post, did Mr. Glavasevic have live shows on the Radio Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did those programmes have any particular name, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the name. They probably did have a name because programming blocks are divided according to their topic or theme, and they each have a name. But I really cannot remember what the names were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what programming block did his programmes belong to. Was it a political programme, cultural programme, news? What did his programmes cover?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They covered all kinds of topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You talked about the programming. Do you know who conceived the programming of Radio Vukovar and Croatian Radio Vukovar in either of the periods of the radio?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly whether it was one person or a team, but this is the job of the editor-in-chief. This is something that the editor-in-chief would do with the assistance of his colleagues, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what was the ethnic composition of the offices of Croatian Radio Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was mixed, but I don't know exactly who was of which ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Since Croatian Radio Vukovar was established, since it was renamed from Radio Vukovar to Croatian Radio Vukovar, do you know how many people worked in the editorial offices or in the offices of Croatian Radio Vukovar since the time you got there in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. A number of the people were employed. Others worked as associates, but I think the number of these associates was larger than the number of those who were actually permanently employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You talked about gathering information, that you gathered information during the events that we have discussing here. Can you please explain to me how you gathered information, how did information reach you at Radio Vukovar or Croatian Radio Vukovar? What were your sources of information?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the events in town. I couldn't really give you all the different sources, but most frequently we talked with the hospital, with the Main Staff, with the people who were out in the field, out at the checkpoints, and there were various sources. The utilities, water works offices, and so on. We talked with the people at Nama, and so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. What was the manner in which you contacted these people? Did you speak to them directly? Did people go to these points that you mentioned, or was there another way of communicating with all these different people and places?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several ways of communicating.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What were they?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was indirect -- I'm sorry, there was direct communication, directly talking with these people. Also it was done through telephone calls. Yes. Well, I can't remember any other way. It was either by telephone or we would go to some places directly or people would come with us and we would talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The premises of the Croatian Radio Vukovar were visited by members of the ZNG. What I'm interested in is that during these encounters did you get any information from them and did you provide information to them? Did you exchange information that each of you had?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did exchange information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what this information was, what kind of information was it?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to describe -- give you examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: But briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A person, a man, a soldier, would come to us or perhaps we would meet somewhere, but most often they would come to us. And we would learn from that man which checkpoint he was at; what was happening there; which people had survived at that point in time, on that day, of course; who was killed; how far the lines of defence were laid down. And then we would talk to them about what was happening at their locations. They didn't really know what was going on in other parts of town, so we would tell them what happened in the other parts of town and what happened to people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that these were military types of information that they provided or that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether that would be military-type of information. These were events in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: But relating to the lines of defence, number of killed, number of casualties, weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So we can agree that --

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as weapons are concerned, well I don't know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So we can agree that this information can have the character or could be of a military nature?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you had frequent contacts with the hospital. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As the radio -- the radio did, but I personally did not have such frequent contacts with the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have anyone specific from Croatian Radio Vukovar who was entrusted with maintaining contacts with hospital representatives, or was this just something that would be on the spur-of-the-moment decision, depending on who was available at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately until the 15th of October it wasn't strictly allocated who would go to the hospital and when. As of the 15th of October when we moved to the Vucedolska Kapljica basement, we organised ourselves and then it was known who was in which shift and in which team. Four persons would be going to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say it was then known who was in which team then. How many teams were there?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me the composition of the teams, each numbers four persons, a total of 12 then?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have 12 persons; we had six. Out of those six we composed three teams. My husband and I were in charge of local programming, which was broadcast three times a day for an hour each time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We seem to have misunderstood each other. I wasn't interested in the programming of Radio Vukovar, I was interested in the people entrusted with contacting the hospital or staying in touch with the hospital.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two teams, each composed of two persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me more about these two teams and their composition.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One was composed of Alenka Mirkovic and Josip Esterajher, the other team comprised Sinisa Glavasevic and Vesna Vukovic. Occasionally they would change teams. Sometimes Sinisa and Josip would go to report on something, but the usual division was Sinisa and Vesna in one team and Josip and Alenka in the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This type of cooperation -- or rather, this type of communication of Croatian Radio Vukovar with the Vukovar Hospital from the 15th of October stayed in place, as far as I understood it, until the 18th of November when you came to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And it operated in certain established time intervals or did you play by ear? Did you go on these reporting assignments twice a week?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. I just remembered something. You said that it stayed in place until the 18th of November, and I have to tell you that Alenka and Josip went to attempt the breakthrough through this siege on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So that means that it stayed in place until the 17th.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, would you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. My question was: Until the 17th of November, 1991, and starting from the 15th of October, 1991, which means a time period of over just more than one month, during that period of time did you have established schedules for these teams to contact the hospital or did you play it by ear?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have established time. It all depended on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of October, 1991, you were in the Vupik shelter?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any kind of communication, except for the direct one, between you - and when I say "you," I mean people in the Vupik basement - and the Vukovar Hospital? Did you have telephone line, radio communication, telex?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no, we didn't have anything. We had to go to the hospital in order to obtain information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that as Croatian Radio Vukovar you had contacts with the Crisis Staff of the Vukovar defence.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were teams established for those contacts as well or was that done by the same two teams?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same two teams did that work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The information you described just a minute ago, was it exchanged in these contacts between you, employees of Croatian Radio Vukovar, the hospital, and the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Dr. Matos mean anything you?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see him ever?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I did, but without knowing that it was him. I don't know what he looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that in the territory of Vukovar there were Croats from all over Croatia who had come from all over Croatia to assist in the defence of Vukovar. Did I understand you right?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People used to come from all over Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had contacts with them?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any information from them about, let's say, the sentiments that prompted them and motivated them to come to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, based on these conversations with them, how were they militarily engaged in the units of the so-called Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't determine that they were in any way different from other local Vukovar residents who were included in the defence of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that they wore uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did they have some insignia in terms of emblems, badges?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Most likely they did, but I couldn't tell you what was written on them, if they had any.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether those who were outside of Vukovar, who had come from elsewhere, were engaged, in the military sense, in the Vukovar defence in such a way that they were all put into one unit or were they perhaps allocated to various units?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what their military assignment was. I didn't know the names of the units, how many there were. I had a feeling that all of those who were involved in the defence functioned as one force, in a unified way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Based on your conversations with these people, were you able to learn whether they fought all in one location, let's say Sajmiste, or were there perhaps some of them who were in Luzac, Mitnica, and other places?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, for a while they fought in one place, in one location. And later on, depending on the situation and the needs, they were transferred to other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You gave evidence about negotiations which were conducted, if I remembered it well, between Mrs. Vesna Bosanac, representing the hospital, and the representatives of the JNA, among whom you've mentioned General Raseta. It remained unclear to me, based on your answers, whether you said that these negotiations were conducted between the 18th and 20th of November, but that there had been some conducted earlier as well. Therefore, I would like you to explain to all of us where these negotiations were conducted and how come you know about any negotiations conducted prior to the 18th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the basement where we were housed, negotiations were conducted; I know this because I saw this and heard this personally. As for the ones conducted between the 18th and the 20th in which Mrs. Bosanac and Marin Vidic, Bili --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Polovina, I was interested in what preceded the 18th.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you also mentioned the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let us just hold on for a minute. So prior to the 18th, who negotiated in the basement with whom and about what?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Vesna Bosanac negotiated with Raseta, who was her counterpart in that telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What were they negotiating about?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They talked about the evacuation of the population. It was clear at that point that the town would fall soon, it was a matter of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please specify in relation to the 17th of September when some of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 17th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: -- when some of the defenders of Vukovar went to break through, including your colleagues. So how long before that date these negotiations were conducted?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The negotiations between Dr. Bosanac and Raseta were not conducted prior to the 17th as far as I know, because I didn't see and didn't hear anything prior to the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So what you're just describing to us perhaps happened on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the earliest on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to Vesna Bosanac, was there anybody else with her present while she talked on the phone and negotiated?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marin Vidic, Bili, was present, and as far as I can remember, Dr. Njavro was there as well. But I'm not sure I can remember their conversations with their counterparts in Zagreb. I seem to remember only the voice of Dr. Vesna Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were any of the defenders of Vukovar present on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, yes, but I can't be certain. There were a number of us in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please explain to me the following. You've already touched upon this, but I'm interested in learning more details. How Croatian Radio Vukovar operated from the moment you moved into the Vupik basement until you went to the hospital. Were there any changes in your programming? Did you have any live programmes? Who was the one who went on air?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 15th of October onwards, so throughout the time we stayed in the basement, we had no live contacts because there were no telephone lines, so it was impossible to have them. Our programme was broadcasted three hours a day, three times, one hour, at 8.00, 2.00 p.m., and 8.00 p.m. Most of that programming was done by me and occasionally some of my colleagues participated as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout that period of time from the 15th of October until the 18th of November when you arrived in the hospital or, let's say, the 17th of November, did you all stay together there? I mean the teams that you have mentioned, the employees.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of us were there together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever, from the 17th on, 17th of November, 1991 -- or rather, after the negotiations held by Dr. Vesna Bosanac, on which occasion Dr. Jure Njavro also was present and perhaps some of the defenders as well, did Dr. Vesna Bosanac ever participate in any broadcasts, ever made any announcements live?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. That's possible. On the 17th we stopped airing, and Sinisa Glavasevic on that day sent -- or rather, broadcast his last reports. I'm not sure what these reports were about. Perhaps they concerned these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The reports that were sent, in order to compile these reports did you use the information obtained in your contacts with the defence staff, hospital, members of the so-called Croatian army, and was this information used in the reports compiled by you?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In which part?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the part which concerned the number of the wounded, dead, the situation at the hospital, how was the defence of the town holding up, which parts of the town had been occupied. Towards the end of November, the town had been cut in half, that is to say there was no communication between the part of the town where the downtown area was and the part near Mitnica. Sajmiste had fallen long time before that. Also, the road between Borovo Naselje and Vukovar had been cut off. All of this was taking place in the course of November, and this is what we informed the population about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This information that was including -- included into your reports, was it censored in any way?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't censored internally, but it was censored by Croatian radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The population of Vukovar, the citizens of Vukovar, covered by your -- the range of the station, did they receive all of the information that you broadcast?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you check in any way this information, or did you just take it for granted that the information given was accurate? Or did you have any reason to doubt the voracity of the information you were receiving from the hospital from the defence Crisis Staff, that you received from the representatives of the defenders of the town?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no doubt about the voracity of the information. The hospital kept daily records of people who were wounded and killed; that can be checked. As far as the number of shells, of course that was not possible to count quite accurately, so we would always give an estimate. This part that we got from the defenders at the checkpoints was something that we could not check. We couldn't go there; it was too dangerous. Before the war it was possible, but after it got very dangerous we couldn't go. We knew some of the things that they had gone through or complete events that had happened to them, and this is something that we would broadcast as we received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that records were lists were kept by the hospital about all this information. Did you see those lists?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see some lists at the very beginning of the war, but after that, no, because I didn't go to the hospital very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe those lists that you saw at the beginning of the war. Were they recorded in a notebook, a pad, on papers?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I think that this information or the names of the people were either sent to us by fax, the names of the killed and the wounded, or when we went to the hospital we would be informed about this, we would be shown a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Since you're not sure about this part, you say that that perhaps arrived by fax.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How -- for how long was it possible to maintain a fax connection between the hospital and the Croatian radio?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August it was functioning. Perhaps up until a certain date in September it functioned. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to me the programming of Croatian Radio Vukovar in the general scheme. These reports, what was their position, what was their role? Was it to inform the citizens? Did it have a propaganda character in order to raise morale of one side in the conflict? Or was it to satisfy someone's interests? Or was it a little bit of each?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This part relating to the programming -- actually, as the war continued, it sort of disappeared. There was no programming scheme. The most important thing became to inform the people in the town what was going on. This was the most important thing, followed by the need to inform the rest of Croatia and the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So the goal was objective informing of the citizens of Vukovar and Croatia, of course.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most important thing to us was to preserve human lives and also to raise the morale of people who were stuck in cellars.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you talked about this, but the explanation still is unclear to me, if that is the way it is, to raise the morale of the defenders. You are also objectively reporting on the events of your town, Vukovar. So according to you what would be the reason of the leadership of Croatia to censor your reports or not to broadcast them as they were to the entire Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to that question; it's entirely speculative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would disagree with the Prosecutor, but I will try to avoid further discussion on this and I will try to ask the witness about this in a different way, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Polovina, do you know what the reason was, did you talk about it amongst yourselves, for the -- these reports being censored, these reports of yours being censored?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did ask ourselves why our reports were being censored, but this is something that only the person who decided to censor the reports is able to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: After your conversations about this, did you try, did anyone, maybe the editor-in-chief, Mr. Glavasevic, try to find out from the people from Croatian radio what the reason was for censoring these reports?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if he received a response? And if he did receive one, what was it and who did he get it from?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he didn't receive a response because whenever he wanted to talk to someone in charge, they were not available. I cannot remember whether he ever actually managed to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to move on to the 17th when you were at the Vupik shelter. You mentioned the arrival of some people from the PTT, the post office. When was this exactly? I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. Maybe it was night-time. I cannot remember what part of the day it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what day it was?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was it a day or two before you went to the hospital? Was it on the same day, the 17th?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- well, I think it was the 17th, but I am not absolutely sure whether it was the 17th or whether it was on the night of the 17th and the 18th. These -- this visit by the guys from the PTT is connected to the departure of the Main Staff from the cellar, so I cannot remember they came before the commander left or if they came afterwards. But I think that it was probably after that. It was the night between the 17th and the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, could you please tell us who these people from the PTT were. What were their names?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Yesterday your colleague mentioned a name, I think it was Zugec. I think he could have been there, but I'm not 100 per cent certain. I think he worked at the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what they were doing, what their jobs were in the post office?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I forgot something. I hope you don't mind if I go back to something that we already talked about relating to the work at Croatian Radio Vukovar. The announcements, reports, or any kind of information, to draft these did you engage any kind of outside assistance? Did you hire people from outside in order to draft these or send messages or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I don't think so, no. We did it all ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of Professor Louc [phoen] From Osijek?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about Professor Medved from Osijek?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the Medved last name a few days ago, but I don't know whether it was the Professor Medved or what context I heard the name. I heard the name a few days ago, but I don't know in what context, and it's not something that I can tie to 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Another thing about the programming. Do you know that Croatian Radio Vukovar, as part of its broadcasting or programming policy from September to November 1991, also featured some kind of educational programme?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who worked on that programme, who anchored the programme or actively participated in it?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was the wife of Dr. Njavro. Her name is Lidija, I think her name is Lidija Njavro, and also the sister of my colleague, Vesna Vukovic. Her name was Melita [phoen]. At the time her last name was Budimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Vesna Vukovic several times. Is that her maiden name or her married name?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is her maiden name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And what is her married last name, if she got married? I think you were her maid of honour, if I understood it properly.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you misunderstood. My best man was Sinisa Glavasevic. Vesna married in January 1992, and her last name is Oreskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was her husband Tomislav Oreskovic?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. His name is Tomislav Oreskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- I have information that you two are very close, so can you explain to the Trial Chamber who Tomislav Oreskovic is and was he in Vukovar at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomislav Oreskovic is Vesna Oreskovic's husband. Her maiden name was Vukovic. He was one of the defenders of Vukovar in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was he only a defender or did he have some kind of command role in the so-called Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are very close, but we really never talked about work all that much. Once he came to Zagreb, and after a considerable time period of treatment he did work in the Croatian army. I think that he did have some kind of rank, but I'm not sure exactly what it's called.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let's move now to the 17th in terms of the agreement to leave Vukovar or breaking out of Vukovar, in the sense that you explained it to us yesterday. You were at Vupik shelter and, as far as I understood, Mr. Glavasevic had gone to the Crisis Staff to see about the terms. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Terms about what?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The terms under which it would be possible to break out, break through.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And what did he say when he returned? That he talked with someone from the Crisis Staff, that the Crisis Staff had gone? What did he say?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he said that he talked with someone from the Main Staff. They had decided to leave town using some routes. At the time it was not really possible -- well, these were routes leading through cornfields because other routes were dangerous. Sinisa came back, said the command was leaving town. Excuse me. That we could go with them, if we wanted to. And that's when we talked about it. We talked about whether we would go or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You already talked about that, but we won't take up too much time. You said that you had decided to stay, where you were. And then on the 18th you went to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's just specify: When did you come to the hospital on the 18th? Was it in the morning, the afternoon, the evening? You did talk about it, but please excuse me for going over it again.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, actually I didn't talk about that yet. I really cannot remember which part of the day it was. I know it was the 18th, but I don't remember what time, what part of the day it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that some civilians came to the Vupik shelter, about a hundred of them, from the fairgrounds, from Sajmiste. Who took you to the hospital? Did anyone take you to the hospital or did you go there yourselves?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we went by ourselves. There was no need for anyone to take us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Before arriving to the hospital, was Marin Vidic with you at the Vupik shelter?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marin Vidic, Bili, did not live at our shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I said that -- I didn't say that he lived at the shelter, but I said shortly before you went to the hospital did he come to the Vupik shelter and then go with you to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I don't think that he did, but I'm not 100 per cent certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me whether these civilians went to the hospital with you or did they stay at the shelter.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilians remained at the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the reason for that? You already had the information that Vukovar was, so to speak, lost, that it would surrender. You, yourself, went to the hospital. Did you say anything to these civilians? Did they inquire about anything?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't say anything to them. We decided to leave the shelter and go to the hospital. The people who remained at the shelter, as far as I know, knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you didn't know what time of the day it was on the 18th when you came to the hospital. As you were walking from the shelter to the hospital, did you see anybody else moving towards the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday when answering the questions of my colleague, Mrs. Tapuskovic, you were shown a map of Vukovar. You put some markings on the map. I'm not going now to trouble either you or the Chamber with the map again, but I will ask you something else. Can you please give us an estimate of the distance between the shelter in which you were, that is to say Vupik shelter, and the hospital. How many metres? Just give us a rough estimate. After all, you studied mathematics and physics, so you must be familiar with measuring?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: 500 metres. And what was the distance between your shelter and the shelter where the Crisis Staff had its headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Less than that. Perhaps 100 to 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood well what you showed and marked on the map, the shelter of the Crisis Staff is closer to the hospital than the shelter in which you were?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell me how far is the Crisis Staff shelter from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 300 to 400 metres. These are just estimates. Not a kilometre, not that far.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I understand that this is just an estimate. What about the MUP building? Where was it in relation to your shelter?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't even remember where they were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the court building is?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know where it is now because I went there just a few days ago, but as for 1991 I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the Vukovar high school building is?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the high school that you completed in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean in that location or in something else? At the time when I attended secondary school, there was no such secondary school. I attended a different type of a secondary school, not a classical gymnasium that you are referring to. My secondary school was near the market, on the other side of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, let us try to put it in these terms. In 1991, was there a classical high school called "gymnasium"?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, I don't know. I attended secondary school between 1981 and 1984. What kind of schools there existed in 1991, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us not waste time.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have a building in Vukovar that we refer to as the building of the classical gymnasium. Now, whether this is the same building that you are interested in --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely the building that I'm interested in. Can you please tell me where it is located in relation to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you leave the hospital and head towards the centre of the town and then head towards Mitnica, on the left side there is the building of the classical gymnasium. This is a hilly area near the Danube. The building of the high school is several kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I will tell you later why I ask this. And if you know the answer, fine; if you don't, just tell us so. You said in your contacts with the hospital representatives you had lists which you received, either via fax or were given them directly when in the hospital. Please tell us, did you have information as to whether members of the National Guards Corps were treated at the hospital as patients who had been wounded or perhaps members of the Croatian defence forces or any other formation? I have to make a comment concerning the transcript. I also added at the end of my question that I was interested in any foreign nationals that might have been treated at the hospital. This should be on page 26, 17 to 18.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a little bit difficult for me to answer this question because I hadn't seen anybody's passport in order to be able to tell you whether they were foreign nationals or not. But yes, there were some people who spoke a mixture of Croatian and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many such people there were there, one or more? Did you see anything yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And how do you know this?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know only of one such person. Now, whether there were more than one, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please describe to me your arrival at the hospital on the 18th. You said that you were put in a room with some doctors; what doctors?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met those people for the first time on that occasion, when I arrived in the hospital. One was called Dr. Vlahovic; I think his first name is Tomislav. The other one is called Dr. Kratofil, from Osijek. The third person was Ante Aric. I don't think he is a physician. I think he was a medical technician. I think he just completed the medical secondary school. We were in a rather small room which had only mattresses and a small cupboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th, when you arrived, did you perhaps tour the hospital that evening? Did you go and see any people? After all, you must have known a lot of people. Did you contact any of them, exchange any information with them there?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I remember touring the hospital, but I don't know whether it was on the 18th or the 19th. I mostly stayed in that room; however, I do remember touring the hospital because I went to see Vesna's then-boyfriend who had been wounded. And on my way to see him, I also visited some other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Vesna's boyfriend, Tomislav, was wounded. Do you remember where? I don't mean which part of his body; I mean location.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Borovo Naselje. I think that he fought near Trpinjska Cesta.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to Vesna Bosanac on the 18th when you arrived in the evening? Did you inquire whether there were any news concerning negotiations or any other news?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember talking to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Dr. Jure Njavro?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably did, but I can't remember all of the persons that I saw during those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing Mr. Marin Vidic, Bili, at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be fully certain that I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, this room in which you were with these two doctors, where is it, in which part of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was definitely on the ground floor, not far from the back entrance. Just a corridor or two corridors away, from the back entrance to the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you say "the back entrance," you have to explain to us how many entrances in the hospital there are. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I know about the main entrance because this is where I entered when I went to visit some of my friends who had stayed in the hospital before the war. So I know about the main entrance, the front entrance, and I learned about the back entrance during those last few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The back entrance, is it something that is not regularly used and is only perhaps used in exceptional circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During peacetime -- I'm not sure. I'm not sure whether people used it or not. I remember always going through the main entrance when I went to the hospital before the war, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, in relation to the main entrance, where is the back entrance? Is it on the opposite side of the building, on another side of the building? Is it on the front facade? Where is it?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The back entrance is not on the same side of the building as the main entrance. The building is between two parallel streets, perpendicular to two parallel streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And this back entrance, what street does it face?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't face any street.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. The 19th, you spent the night at the hospital. Did anything particular happen at the hospital on the 18th? Was it an eventful day?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see anything; however, I heard that people wearing uniforms - I'm not sure what uniforms - had entered the hospital. I'm not sure whether it was on the 18th or the 19th. This is nothing remarkable, but if you are asking me to remember what happened during those days, I can tell you that I remember lying in the room the whole time and going out maybe once or twice to see Vesna's husband. I heard that people in uniforms started entering hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you went to visit Vesna's hospital, Tomislav Oreskovic, were there any other familiar faces there who also came to visit him?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. Most likely yes, but I don't remember. I only remember Tomislav.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Filip Karaula ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what did you hear and how is he known to you?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that he had fought at Mitnica. I think that he was either one of the commanders or the commander, defence commander, at Mitnica. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, 1991, you were at the hospital. Did you have any information whatsoever while at the hospital, did you receive any information from people you had contacts with, or did you receive this information from any other source about what had happened to Filip Karaula and the people at Mitnica? Did anything happen to them; and if so, what? I'm trying not to put a leading question.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I know that in those last few days Mitnica had been cut off. There was no communication with them. I can't remember hearing anything. Later on, I saw it in the media, but back then, during those last days, no, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So no information reached you about the Mitnica Battalion surrendering on the 18th of November to the members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. Possibly yes, but I can't be fully certain. I can't tell you, yes, such-and-such person told me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't expecting you to tell me precisely who provided this information to you. I was just interested in learning whether you had heard of this back then.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I heard it on that day or later, upon leaving Vukovar, because, you know, these things are not quite clear in my mind anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You went to the hospital. What was the reason for your going there? Was it because you had heard that there would be negotiations about the evacuation of the hospital and people within it? Or was it that you had heard information that the population of Vukovar would be evacuated? So these are two different things.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither of the two reasons. If I had to choose, then it would be the evacuation of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If it is the evacuation of the population, then did you hear that the population would be evacuated from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The ethnic structure of the people who were in these shelters, for example, the shelter in Vupik where you were, what was the ethnic structure there?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I think that it was mixed. Mostly it was people of the -- of Croat ethnicity, but there were some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Which others?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those who lived in the area of the Vukovar municipality. It was a multi-ethnic community, so I don't really know exactly. I think there were Ukrainians, Ruthenians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please answer whether there were any Serbs among these people.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but I don't know whether there were any or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly. It's not possible to distinguish.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not -- I cannot distinguish a man or a person when I see them according to their nationality. I don't know what nationality they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was anything happening on the 19th in the morning at the Vukovar Hospital which made an impression on you? Something that has stuck in your mind, something that you remember happened on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remembered one soldier. I mentioned him yesterday, but I don't know whether this was on the 19th in the morning or what part of the day. But I think that it was on the 19th. This soldier with the Krajina militia insignia, but I cannot remember anything else other than hearing that some people were being taken away from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Where was this? Was it in the morning? At Noon? Afternoon? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Zeljko or Zeljka Zgonjanin mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: It's Zeljka?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Zeljka Zgonjanin, a woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who was Zeljka Zgonjanin?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljka Zgonjanin I think is from the Red Cross. I cannot exactly say what she was, president, secretary. Perhaps she didn't have any particular title, but I think that she was doing something in the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Zeljka Zgonjanin at the Vukovar Hospital on the 19th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I did. I remember being with her during those last days when I was still in Vukovar, but I don't know whether this was on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, when you saw her, what was she doing in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is it perhaps time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at quarter past, and of course then finish at quarter to 1.00. Could I mention while we're -- quarter to 2.00. Could I mention that while we're dealing with this, on Monday, next, we will be sitting at 2.15, but there is a special plenary of Judges at 4.00, so that we will have only the one session from 2.15 until 3.45, if that affects your planning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Polovina, we'll continue where we left off. The 19th of November, 1991, you were at the hospital in a room where I think you said there were two [as interpreted] doctors, Mr. Vlahovic, Mr. Kratofil, Ante Aric, and you don't know who the third doctor who was there. Who was there with you from Croatian Radio Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branimir Polovina was there, Sinisa Glavasevic, and Vesna Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did any of the persons who were mentioned, other than the doctors, Vlahovic, Kratofil, and this third doctor whose name you don't know, leave the room and the 20th, in the morning?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does "until 20th, in the morning" mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: From the point you came until that morning.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All four of us would leave the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How much time did you spend outside of the room?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Myself, personally, very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about the others?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did go out of the room on several occasions, but I really couldn't say. We're talking about hours, so perhaps a few hours on that one day, the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The 19th, in the evening, on the eve of the 20th, were you all together in that room?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk about where they were for that -- for those couple of hours on the 19th, what they did, whether they saw anything or heard anything?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you anything interesting about the events on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went to see the wounded who were lying in the hospital. They stopped to see some of their friends, acquaintances, talked with them. I found out from them that negotiations were underway or that the negotiations went on that day, and then in the evening I found out what time we had to leave the hospital the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th you also left the room and went around the hospital. Did you notice the presence of a large number of civilians at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of them practically were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the approximate number of civilians who were staying at the hospital on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot because I didn't go to see all of these civilians. No, I cannot tell you. I went to the place where Tomislav was lying, but I didn't really go into all of the corridors and the shelters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Which parts of the hospital did you go to see, if for no other reason then out of journalistic curiosity?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember. All of this was -- when I say "parts," I mean the areas, the corridors, the rooms. It was all in the -- in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: Earlier you would enter the hospital by the main entrance? Earlier.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war. And then from the main entrance you enter some sort of, perhaps hall, and then the corridors, the entry part of the building?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there is some kind of a staircase when you enter by this main entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So in these corridors, we're talking about the 19th, in this main entrance area, were there civilians in these corridors?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in that part of the hospital on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Do you know whether, other than this entrance and exit which you came in by or went out by on the 18th, are there any other exits or entrances in the immediate vicinity?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there are, but I cannot be 100 per cent certain. There was no official exit or entrance; that was evident.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the street, does this entrance that you're talking about look out on some street?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which street do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The same entrance that you entered on the 18th and that you exited on on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it facing any street? I don't know -- no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information in relation to the 19th of November that members of the Yugoslav People's Army entered the hospital, together with representatives of the International Red Cross, on the 19th of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of November, 1991, did you notice journalists, your colleagues, from foreign television stations taping or filming inside the hospital, in the area where there were wounded persons, civilians, the staff?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that there were members of the media talking in the hospital with any of the hospital staff on the 19th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: From your colleagues and the people who were with you in that room and who left the room to see their friends, the wounded, civilians, did you find out that what I just told you was actually happening at the hospital, that the army had arrived and representatives of international organisations, foreign camera crews?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from my colleagues that enemy soldiers had entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That's all?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have information in -- did you obtain information in any other way that on the 19th of November, 1991, a humanitarian convoy had arrived at the Vukovar Hospital under the auspices of the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have information or did you have information on the 19th of November that on that day, under the auspices of the Red Cross, whose secretary was the woman that we mentioned, Zeljka Zgonjanin, civilians were evacuated from the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the 19th of November, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have this information or not?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have this information then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So the 19th, in the evening, bedtime, let's say, was it, again, the same people who were in that room, Ante Aric, Kratofil, Vlahovic, and this fourth doctor, and the Vukovar Radio staff?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people from the radio were there, but I'm not sure about the other four. All four of them were with us -- I'm not sure if all four of them were with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Now, regarding Mr. Glavasevic and the 18th, in your statement you said that Sinisa sent in his broadcast on the 18th of November in the evening to Zagreb. What kind of a programme was it? Was it an audio-recording or what?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a programme. I think it's a question of interpretation. It was a report, a telephone report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So it was a telephone report.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about the B/C/S version. It's possible that the translation is bad, but now it's clear. Could you please tell us, if you remember, who gave you the information on the 19th in the evening at what time you should be ready on the 20th, and why did you need -- would you need to be ready?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I'm not sure whether Sinisa or Branko told me, but they had the information. But I didn't only hear it from them. I heard it from some other people who were present, some of the doctors, because some people would enter the room. We went out into the corridor in front of the room, so I don't know exactly who it was that told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And what did they tell you to be ready for?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me that the next morning we would be leaving, that the citizens would be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did they answer -- or did they explain why this evacuation was being conducted? Was it based on some kind of agreement, accord? Was it just spontaneous? Was it organised? Who was organising it?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me that negotiations were conducted and that this was agreed on, that it would be an organised evacuation. That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Now we're gradually moving to the 19th --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, we're moving to the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And I'm actually very interested in the 20th, it's what interests me the most. On the 19th, in the evening, did anything happen at the hospital that would indicate the existence of any problems? Was there rushing around, a kind of chaotic situation, anything like that? Or was everything normal, as far as it could be normal in those conditions for the preparation of such an operation like that, that was supposed to begin the next day?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it normal. All of us were afraid about what was going to happen because we heard that some people had been taken away from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The 20th, in the morning, you say that you woke up at 7.00?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At around 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: 7.00. Mr. Glavasevic left. Do you know who remained with you in the room? Were the doctors there?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that Ante Aric was there. As for the others, I don't know. I know for a fact that Branimir Polovina and Vesna Vukovic were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Ante Aric several of times. Can you tell me, how was he dressed, do you remember, on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I think he had a white coat and pants, but I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In terms of his white coat, did he have a white suit or -- you don't know. All right. You say that you left the room at around 8.00 and then you went out through the back entrance, as you had been told. This is what your statement says, the statement given to the OTP. I'm interested in learning who told you that, to go out through the back entrance, and where were you told this?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We lay in that room, the room where we were upon arriving in the hospital. I can't remember whether we opened the door, whether there was any door, but at any rate very close to our room -- I don't know whether I was still lying in the room or that was in the corridor. The room was just crowded with mattresses. It wasn't a very comfortable room, and there were no other chairs. We could just lie on mattresses. And then one soldier came and said, "You have to leave." I had an impression that he was tasked with checking whether there were any people left in the rooms, and this is how he came to our room and told us we had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said "a soldier"?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Whose soldier?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that you're no expert for military issues. I'm just interested in learning whether that was an ordinary soldier or somebody who held a rank.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that he held a rank. I think he was just a rank-and-file soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see next to this rank-and-file soldier any other troops in the corridor in front of the room where you stayed? Were there any other troops there?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And then you left. Once you left and went outside, were there already people standing there in front of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: After your departure, did other people come out of the hospital or were you the last ones to leave it?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be positive about it. I can't say whether anybody remained back. There were people outside, and my impression was that we were among the last ones so leave but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, among the people who were outside in front of the hospital -- you're not sure whether these people left with you or not, but did you see any doctors among these people?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I can remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the doctors?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, as I was leaving the hospital, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's define one thing, just to be clear about the timing. You woke up at around 7.00, and what time was it when you left the hospital? It could have been what time?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was at about 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: At about 8.00. Did you know - and if so, who did you learn it from - that at the time the doctors had been invited to attend the medical staff meeting at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that. When I left the hospital, there were many women around me. We started talking, and then I learned that the medical staff had gone to discuss something.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where these discussions of the medical staff with somebody else were taking place?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who they discussed with, the medical staff?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, no. I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "at the time, no," does that mean that at some other time, later, you learned who they had discussed this with?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this, but I saw this later on television. I think that I also heard it in that convoy as we were travelling to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what did you hear on television? Was it something related to the discussions of the medical staff?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.
