utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe it to us.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't the meeting of the medical staff. It's just that I heard that Dr. Bosanac and Marin Vidic, Bili, went somewhere with Sljivancanin to discuss something.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On that morning?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the 20th in the morning.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 20th in the morning, I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because in your statement -- if you don't remember it, I can give you the statement. I will read this out correctly, trust me. It says in your statement as follows. "At 8.00 in the morning, we left the room and we went out of the hospital through the back entrance, as we had been told. I was with Vesna Vukovic and my husband. At the same time, three doctors were invited to attend the meeting between the medical staff and the JNA representatives." Did you state this?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely why I asked you this. In 1995 this is what you told the investigators. So you had this information, and if you had this information did you also know who were these JNA representatives who had a meeting with the medical staff and what did they discuss?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you came out of the hospital on the 20th in the morning, you say that you "saw" -- my husband [as interpreted] -- "Mr. Sljivancanin then."

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to him, did you see any other members of the military, any other officers or was he the only one?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some other soldiers there, members of the military. He wasn't the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were these people with ranks?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know whether they had any ranks. I just assumed that there is a certain hierarchy in the army and that everybody has to have a rank or hold a post of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And this is where you separated?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't separate on our own. We were separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Please don't take me wrong. I meant no harm by saying so. You were told to separate. First you mentioned four groups, then you mentioned two groups. You said that you were not mistreated but were told to take out some items from your bags, namely all sharp objects. Would you please tell me who told you this and who did this, if something like this was done.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How many of you were there outside? 250? 300? 100?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Less than that. Not more than a hundred, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was there just one soldier who was inspecting your bags and confiscating sharp objects, or were there several soldiers doing that?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several of them but not too many, perhaps three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that there were wounded among them who stood there?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Among the people standing outside in front of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you say that you saw Ante Aric there as well?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not allowed to talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you didn't talk as you stood there. Who prevented you from talking?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veselin Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So from 8.00, when you left the hospital, until you departed from there, Veselin Sljivancanin stood there the whole time?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not sure that he stood there the entire time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice on the 20th, in the morning, the JNA ambulances being parked there in front of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. When we stood there, separated, in front of the hospital, no, not in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you gave a statement to the Prosecutor, you said "some men walked around even though they had been wounded. Some were seriously wounded." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: "As far as I know, those who were seriously wounded were taken in an ambulance to Zagreb." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So when were these seriously wounded people taken to Zagreb in ambulances? I just refreshed your memory?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did, but you're talking about the 20th in the morning. Those who were seriously wounded were taken to Zagreb in the same convoy in which I travelled, so I was on a bus.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had an impression that you interrupted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. So the bus that I was travelling on, naturally with other people, there were other women and children there, was followed by several ambulances carrying the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that after that, European observers came. You said that they had come from the opposite side of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I say "the opposite side," I'm referring to the side which is opposite the side where the men stood from where they were taken. That was in the late morning. I'm not sure about the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that several foreign journalists came at the same time?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And then you say that they were able to talk to whomever they wanted?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's right because I saw some women from my group talking to journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That means that somebody remained in front of the hospital, not all of you were boarded on buses, if they were able to stay there and talk to them?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're saying. The men were taken away. They turned a corner. Us women, we remained standing there; I don't know for how long. And then after that, European monitors and foreign journalists came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said they could talk to anybody they wanted, but they mostly talked to officers and doctors. How many officers, in your view, were there?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Two? Three? Five?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that all of them were officers. I guess an officer implies a rank. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that they were officers in that case. They wore uniforms. Ten at the most. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that they talked to JNA officers and doctors. Can I conclude, based on that, that in front of the hospital there were JNA officers and doctors standing together?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I don't think so. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Amongst the doctors of the Vukovar Hospital who were standing in front of the hospital, did you happen to see any members of the Yugoslav People's Army, an officer wearing a white coat over his uniform?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since you were at the hospital frequently or, let's say -- frequently, I mean you have contacts with people in the hospital, did you know a doctor by the name of Mladen Ivankovic?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On the 20th, amongst the doctors, did you see Dr. Njavro and Dr. Vesna Bosanac at the hospital, on the 20th, or in front of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, but I don't remember. I don't think so, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You were at the Vukovar Hospital from the 18th, you don't know from exactly what time, until the morning of the 20th. You had contacts with Mr. Marin Vidic, Bili, the president of the Crisis Staff. You had contacts with representatives of the town defenders. You exchanged information for the purposes of providing information to the public. And I'm interested: Did you ever hear that between the Vukovar Crisis Staff and the Vukovar Hospital staff there was a plan made about attempting to save as many members of the ZNG as possible, also of the military police and the MUP, during the evacuation? And this was agreed on in the following that: That a group of the members of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia would be placed on the list of the working group, which was allegedly servicing the hospital; that another group would be issued with certificates of wounding; and that their uniforms would be hidden. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very long sentence -- actually, it's several sentences. You began by mentioning the period from the 18th to the 20th, that I was in contact with Marin Vidic, Bili, and Dr. Bosanac. I cannot actually remember having contacts with them in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, we didn't understand each other.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just looked at the screen and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we didn't understand each other.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned the period between the 18th and the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This is in connection with your arrival at the hospital which means --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers not overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned the date I arrived at the hospital and I was in contact with Marin Vidic, Bili, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let's try this way -- yes, it was a long sentence. From the contacts that you had as somebody who was employed at the Croatian Radio Vukovar and which were maintained with the Crisis Staff, with the Vukovar Hospital, with representatives of the National Guards Corps, did you have any information about a plan being agreed on, namely a plan being made, how, during the evacuation, to save as many members of the National Guards Corps, the MUP, and military police as possible?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about this while you were staying at the hospital on the 18th from an unspecified time and then the whole day and night of the 19th and then the 20th in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the utmost respect, the witness has answered this question. It's being asked just in a different way because the Defence got an answer they do not wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The first answer does appear to cover the whole period from the 18th to the 20th, Mr. Bulatovic. That's certainly the way we would understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Polovina, I see from your personal data that you completed high school in 1984 and that you studied in Osijek, that you left your studies in 1989. In the period from 1989 until 1990, were you continually in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: During that time that you spent in Vukovar and also during the time that you spent these two time periods working at Radio Vukovar and Croatian Radio Vukovar, you are sure to have met many people and gotten to know many people who were important in the life of the town of Vukovar. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did meet these people, but I really didn't get to know them all that well. Mostly I spent time with my long-term friends. I didn't really get very close to the people that I met in this capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to tell you several names of people that I'm interested in, and if you have heard of these people could you please tell me, first of all, whether you have heard of these people and what you know about them. I asked you about Filip Karaula. Did you hear about a name called -- a man called Blago Zadro?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What did you hear? Who is that man? What does he do? What is his profession?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blago Zadro is no longer living. He was killed at Trpinjska Cesta, I think sometime in October. He was a commander of the defence of Borovo Naselje. I think he was the commander of that sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: As journalists -- as a journalist of Croatian Radio Vukovar, did you have any contacts with him?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, telephone contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Josip Gazo mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I heard of the Gazo last name. The name Josip I know, it's known to me, but those two names together I really cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about Stipan Radas?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of a person named Vlado Rimac?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of the last name Rimac, but the name Vlado with the last name Rimac doesn't ring any bells.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the name Ivo Madjarevic?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivo Madjarevic, no, I cannot recall that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of Franjo Mujic?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about Branko Krizmaric?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about Slobodan Mandic?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about Franjo Djurica, the chief of the police administration in Vukovar at a certain period, if I may assist you?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of the Djurica last name, but those two names together, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Ferencz, Kovac?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What did you hear about him?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man worked at the registry office and he performed the marriage ceremony when he I married my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of a person called Ivica Franic, nicknamed Srna, if that means anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of the Srna nickname, but I haven't heard of Ivica Franic. I cannot connect it to that name. But I did hear of Srna.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What did you hear about that nickname? Who does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that it was a person who was a fighter in the Vukovar defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of a person called Ivica Arbanas?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What did you hear about him?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He also was a fighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Marin Pliso?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pliso, that last name is familiar to me but I really don't know what the first name is of the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Stipo Pole?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What did you hear about Stipo Pole?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stipo Pole worked at the police. He was one of the commanders I think or a chief or -- or someone who was in the police leadership in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about Milenko Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I have one more name. Did you hear of Ante Roso?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not while I was in Vukovar. This is a name that I became more familiar with after the war from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in Vukovar you never heard of that name?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: As a journalist, a person whose business is objective reporting - that's the function of the media - you have certain contacts. So based on the contacts that you have, do you have any information about the relations in the Crisis Staff of the Vukovar defence vis-a-vis the Republic of Croatia and also the relationships between people performing certain functions within the Crisis Staff? Was everything functioning as it was supposed to? Were there any misunderstandings? And if there were, what they were about? And did you report about any of these misunderstandings between anyone?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not receive such information from the people who were at the staff, but I did hear that their -- I heard that the relationships were not so good towards the end. I heard this from my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I have my last question now, and I think that will be sufficient. If you know, please tell me: Do you know anything about the activities of Tomislav Mercep in relation to Serbs in Vukovar? About arrests of prominent Serbs, killings of Serbs, the mining of Serb houses, and any kind of intimidation?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much. I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bulatovic. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one matter before my learned friend perhaps concludes. Really, it relates to cross-examination vis-a-vis the morning of the 20th. Of course the witness said that Mr. Sljivancanin was outside - this is in chief - and was spoken to by ladies about what was happening to the men and an explanation given by Major Sljivancanin to those wives. That has not been dealt with by my learned friend. Can I take it then that it is accepted by the Defence that that was said by Major Sljivancanin? Because the witness should have an opportunity, if that is going to be disputed, the witness must have an opportunity of clarifying that matter and having an ability to reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, if no Defence counsel pursues that issue, the expectation is that it is not disputed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If that's the Court's view, then I have no problems with that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I'll pause in case some Defence counsel wishes to dispute it, but I think I've found one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps, it's not right. My colleague was asking the questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, perhaps he should take over. We don't change horses in the middle of a gallop.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I absolutely understand my learned friend from the Prosecution, what he's seeking with this objection. But my line of questions was directed at establishing the presence of Mr. Sljivancanin and certain places. So I think that in the course of the proceedings we will continue also to prove this. I am not disputing the fact that my client was there on the 20th. Whether he was in all the places throughout that whole period is something else. I think the statement of this witness is saying something which is quite different from what the Prosecutor is asserting. However, later in the course of the proceedings we will seek to establish that. I cannot have a person violating all the laws of physics and space in that sense, if it were -- if it was to be the way the Prosecution is claiming. But we will continue to pursue this as we continue with the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Moore, you can take it that the subject matter of the conversation is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But would the Court just hear my submission for a short -- a short submission in relation to it? With the utmost respect to my learned friends, there are two issues here: One whether Major Sljivancanin was present when individuals were taken from the hospital at, let us say, the morning; and two, that Major Sljivancanin was spoken to by women who inferentially were concerned about their husbands. And a reply was given -- a reply was given. We would submit that is a significant conversation, and inferences could be drawn in relation to that reply. Now, if my learned friend is going to submit later on about Major Sljivancanin, these two areas, in my submission, must be dealt with now. Firstly, was Sljivancanin there or not? And secondly, if he was there, did he have such a conversation and indicate that, in actual fact, the men were going to be separated from the women, taken to the JNA barracks, and then re-united? Because the Prosecution case has always been that this was a deliberate attempt to placate individuals, isolate the men who were then subsequently killed. It is one of the key issues of the case, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. As I have indicated, there has been no suggestion to the contrary in the course of cross-examination by three Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I deal with short points on re-examination -- at least I hope they'll be short points. Madam --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It looks, Mr. Moore, that Mr. Bulatovic wants to say more.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think that Mr. Moore understood me. If, at this point in time, we accepted to proceed in this manner, establish things or not establish things, then all of us should be on one side. It is up to the Trial Chamber to assess what has been established based on each testimony. At this point in time, I do not wish and I am not going to give this assessment. I'm going to do this when the time comes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So that there can be no misunderstanding in the future, the subject matter of Mr. Moore's observation and the Chamber's indication of the position arises out of Rule 90(H), subparagraph ii, which requires that: "In cross-examination of a witness, counsel shall put to that witness the nature of the case of the party for whom that counsel appears and which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness." That being so, there having been nothing put to this witness to suggest that there was not that conversation and that its content was not as the witness has indicated, the understanding of the Chamber is that those matters are not in dispute. That's the sole point of what has been discussed. The Chamber is in no way indicating that there are final findings of fact being made at this point or that it will not be open to the Defence to put its case and to put submissions following that. It's just that on an issue of this nature, if it really is the case of any member of the Defence teams -- sorry, any one of the Defence teams that there was no such a conversation that morning, then that needs to have been put to the witness. Now, with the air all clear about that, Mr. Moore, if you would carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Madam, you told us about the convoy when you left on the 20th, the convoy that you travelled on. That was the convoy that you described having the ambulances. How many men travelled on that convoy with you, if you can assess percentage-wise?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say with accuracy because I was on the bus and it was only women on the bus with me. As the convoy travelled, the buses were moving and I kept looking back because Veselin Sljivancanin had said that the men would go to the barracks for a brief questioning and then would follow us. Therefore, I kept looking back to see if there were any additional vehicles joining our convoy and travelling with us to Zagreb. Based on that, on that looking back, I know that there were several ambulances carrying the wounded. There is another issue, which is that at one point in time when we arrived in Vojvodina, my colleague, Vesna Vukovic, who had travelled with me up to that time, moved into the vehicle in which her husband who was wounded was travelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we talk about the convoy itself and the travelling from Vukovar, did there come a time when the buses disembarked, when people got off the buses?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity of seeing how many men or women actually got off those buses?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't be able to say because we disembarked, and I'm not sure whether that was in Sremska Mitrovica or we had already reached Novi Sad. I really don't remember. I know that we were allowed to get off the buses at one point. I can remember that. But how many people, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I didn't ask about people. I asked about the division between male and female. Are you able to assess the percentage of male or female --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm objecting to this line of questioning of my learned friend because I don't see how this arises or what this arises from. These issues were not brought up by any of the Defence counsel during cross-examinations. None of the Defence teams asked the witness in cross-examination about the movement of convoy after it left Vukovar and travelled to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The witness gave evidence about convoys, but in any event the issue, the core issue, of this witness's evidence -- one of the core issues is the fact that men were taken away and went around the corner and that there had been separation. And all three of my learned friends cross-examined on that issue, as far as I can recollect. But in any event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But, Mr. Moore, how does it arise for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It arises for re-examination because in our submission the Court would be entitled to know whether in actual fact separation has been occurred and not merely was intended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Isn't that subject of evidence in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is a matter for evidence in chief and it was dealt with in chief vis-a-vis the separation. But in our submission it arises out of the cross-examination because the witness herself was asked about ambulances and whether in actual fact ambulances escorted the convoy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But to say, Mr. Moore, that -- in my view it's not a matter for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, have you been left alone too long. I'm sorry, I'm not ignoring you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. You pre-empted what I was going to say. I have nothing to add to that. I just wanted to applaud what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You were asked about the exchange of material between the hospital and the Crisis Staff. Do you remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exchange of material? You mean information?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What sort of information was exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information about the number of the dead, wounded, even some individual cases were discussed. We would receive information about what had happened to an individual person. So it wasn't just the figures that we were given. We also received information about the situation in the hospital, the supply of medication, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Finally this, it's really a point of clarification as much as anything. In evidence in chief, that was replying questions to myself, you were asked about Sajmiste and you seemed to suggest that that had -- that part of the town had been taken, to use your words, in the first half of September. In cross-examination, it seems to be that you were suggesting that that area fell on the -- on and around the 15th of October. I can give the page numbers if it assists my learned friends. Can you, for clarification, please, tell the Court, if you know, actually when it was that Sajmiste had been taken. Was it September or was it another occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Sajmiste was not occupied and did not fall on one particular day. We can't pick a day when that happened. I think it went house by house or street by street. It was a gradual process. These people who arrived after the 15th of October into our basement had been staying in a shelter in Sajmiste. I don't know where this shelter was, whether it was close to the town or not. I don't know how combat operations unfolded and on what day a particular part of Sajmiste fell. It was a gradual process. It took some time for that to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know where the JNA barracks in Vukovar is located, the area of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZVEZDANA POLOVINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is near Sajmiste, in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Polovina, you'll be pleased to know that that is the end of your questioning, the end of your evidence. You'll be now free to return to your home. The Chamber would thank you for coming to The Hague and for the assistance you've given. You may now go with the court officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The next witness is Mara Bucko. I'm entirely in the Court's hands whether it's appropriate to start now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: 14 minutes, given a minute or two to get her, we'd certainly manage 12 minutes. Do you think that would be useful?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: For my part, I think not. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You think not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think -- I'm quite willing to assist my learned friends. So there's no mystery about it, it was our intention in the witness list to call her husband first. For various reasons, Your Honour will see also that there was another witness called Koprcina, and we re-appraised the case and we informed my learned friends some time ago we would not be calling that witness. There was an element of duplication. So, as an element of that, we brought witnesses forward. So we saved a day and a half in relation to that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's the first good news the Chamber has had for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There's other good news, but you don't know about it. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well then. I think we might call it an early finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's very tricky to start a long witness just a few minutes short of the day. So we will resume again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 2nd day of December, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
